summary: Describes a mechanism for providing cryptographic authentication for IPv4 and IPv6 datagrams. It is the original Authentication Header specification, later replaced by RFC 2402.

plainLanguage.summary: The Authentication Header is an extra IP header that carries a cryptographic fingerprint of a datagram. The sender computes it over the whole packet and the receiver recomputes it, so a packet that was altered or forged in transit is detected and dropped. It does not encrypt anything, so it proves who sent a packet but not what was in it.

how does ah authenticate ip packets
how does authentication work in ip
subtitle: An IP header that proves a datagram was not altered on the way, and where it came from.

tldr.problem: On the Internet, a receiving host has no way to tell whether a datagram really came from the host it claims to come from, or whether something along the path altered it.
tldr.mechanism: The Authentication Header carries a value computed over the whole datagram by a cryptographic algorithm, with the fields that routers change in transit treated as zero. The receiver recomputes the value and compares it.
tldr.outcome: A receiver can drop any datagram whose authentication value does not match, and log the failure. The header gives no confidentiality, so it authenticates but does not hide. It has been replaced by RFC 2402.

today: RFC 1826 was a Proposed Standard published in August 1995. It has been obsoleted by RFC 2402, which is the current specification of the IP Authentication Header.

sections.title: What the Authentication Header Does
sections.content:
The Authentication Header is a mechanism for providing strong integrity and authentication for IP datagrams. It might also provide non-repudiation, depending on which cryptographic algorithm is used and how keying is performed: use of an asymmetric digital signature algorithm such as RSA could provide non-repudiation.

Confidentiality, and protection from traffic analysis, are not provided by the Authentication Header. Users desiring confidentiality should consider using the IP Encapsulating Security Protocol (ESP) either in lieu of or in conjunction with the Authentication Header.

The mechanism adds authentication information to an IP datagram. The information is calculated using all of the fields in the datagram that do not change in transit, which includes not only the IP header but also other headers and the user data. Fields or options that need to change in transit, such as hop count, time to live, ident, fragment offset or routing pointer, are considered to be zero for the calculation. This provides significantly more security than is currently present in IPv4 and might be sufficient for the needs of many users.

Using the header increases the IP protocol processing costs in participating end systems and increases the communications latency, because the sender calculates the authentication data and the receiver calculates and compares it for every datagram that carries the header.

To work without changing the entire Internet infrastructure, the authentication data is carried in its own payload, and systems that are not participating in the authentication may ignore the Authentication Data. With IPv6 the header is normally placed after the Fragmentation and End-to-End headers and before the ESP and transport-layer headers. With IPv4 it immediately follows the IPv4 header.
sections.plainLanguage: The header proves that a datagram arrived unchanged and was sent by the party that claims to have sent it. It says nothing about what the datagram contained, because the contents are not encrypted.

sections.title: Security Associations and Key Management
sections.content:
Key management is an important part of the IP security architecture, but it is not integrated with this specification, because of a long history in the public literature of subtle flaws in key management algorithms and protocols. The Authentication Header tries to decouple the key management mechanisms from the security protocol mechanisms. The only coupling between the two is the Security Parameters Index (SPI).

The key management mechanism negotiates a number of parameters for each Security Association, including the keys and other information such as the authentication algorithm and mode. It creates and maintains a logical table containing those parameters for each current security association, and an implementation reads that table to decide how to process each datagram that carries an Authentication Header.

Security Associations are unidirectional, so a bidirectional session normally has one association in each direction: for a TCP session between two systems A and B there is normally one Security Association from A to B and a separate one from B to A. The receiver assigns the SPI value to the Security Association with that sender, and the other parameters are determined in a manner specified by the key management mechanism. Because several key management mechanisms can be used, and because the key management protocol can be changed without unduly impacting the security protocol implementations, the decoupling permits either to evolve.
sections.plainLanguage: The keys and the algorithm live in a table of Security Associations, one per direction of travel. The header carries only a number that says which row of that table to use, so the key management can be changed without changing the header format.

sections.title: The Header Syntax and Its Fields
sections.content:
The Authentication Header may appear after any other headers that are examined at each hop, and before any other headers that are not examined at an intermediate hop. The IPv4 or IPv6 header immediately preceding it carries the value 51 in its Next Header, or Protocol, field.

The header has five parts. Next Header is 8 bits wide and identifies the next payload after the Authentication Payload, using the set of IP Protocol Numbers. Payload Length is 8 bits wide and gives the length of the Authentication Data field in 32-bit words; the minimum value is 0 words, used only in the degenerate case of a null authentication algorithm. Reserved is 16 bits wide, reserved for future use, and MUST be set to all zeros when sent; the value is included in the calculation but otherwise ignored by the recipient.

Security Parameters Index is a 32-bit pseudo-random value identifying the security association for this datagram. The value 0 is reserved to indicate that no security association exists, and the values 1 through 255 are reserved to IANA. Authentication Data has a variable length that is always an integral number of 32-bit words. Many implementations require padding to other alignments, such as 64 bits, to improve performance, and all implementations MUST support such padding, which is specified by the destination on a per SPI basis. The padding value is chosen by the sender and is included in the calculation. If the field is longer than needed for the actual authentication data, the unused bit positions are filled with unspecified, implementation-dependent values.
sections.plainLanguage: The header carries the number of the security association, a length and the authentication value itself. Fields that routers must change, such as the time to live, are set to zero for the calculation so that the receiver can reproduce it.

sections.title: Calculating and Checking the Authentication Data
sections.content:
The authentication data is usually calculated using a message digest algorithm such as MD5, either encrypting that digest or keying the digest directly. Only algorithms believed to be cryptographically strong one-way functions should be used, and conventional checksums such as CRC-16 MUST NOT be used because they are not cryptographically strong.

The sender first locates the appropriate Security Association, selecting it at least on the sending userid and the Destination Address. Fields that necessarily change during transit and whose value at the receiver is not known with certainty by the sender, such as TTL and the header checksum for IPv4 or the Hop Limit for IPv6, are included in the calculation but are processed specially: the value carried in the packet is replaced by zero. Replacing the value with zero rather than omitting the fields preserves alignment for the calculation.

The sender MUST compute the authentication over the packet as that packet will appear at the receiver, so that future IP optional headers the receiver might not know about still work, and so that data that varies in transit but whose value at the final receiver is known in advance can be authenticated. The calculated digest goes into the Authentication Data field, and for the purpose of the computation that field is considered to be filled with zeros.

In IPv4, the Time to Live and Header Checksum fields are the only base header fields handled specially, and they MUST be set to all zeros for the calculation. Because IPv4 packets are subject to intermediate fragmentation in routers, reassembly of IPv4 packets must be performed prior to the Authentication Header processing, and IPv4 implementations SHOULD use Path MTU Discovery. The IP Security Option MUST be included in the calculation whenever it is present. If a receiving system does not recognise an IPv4 option that is present, that option is included in the calculation, so any IPv4 packet containing an option that changes during transit in an unpredictable manner and that the receiver does not recognise will fail the check and be dropped.

In IPv6, the Hop Limit is the only base header field handled specially, and all IPv6 option type values contain a bit that determines whether the option data is included in the calculation: if that bit is zero the option is included, and if it is one the option is replaced by zero bits of the same length. The IPv6 Routing Header Type 0 rearranges address fields during transit, but the contents of the packet as it will appear at the receiver are known to the sender, so that header is included using the normal procedure.

On receipt, the receiver uses the Destination Address and the SPI value to locate the correct Security Association, then independently verifies that the Authentication Data field and the received packet are consistent. If the algorithm indicates the datagram is valid it is accepted. If the data and the header do not match, the receiver SHOULD discard the datagram as invalid and MUST record the failure in the system log or audit log. The recorded log data MUST include the SPI value, the date and time received, the clear-text sending address, the clear-text destination address and, if it exists, the clear-text Flow ID.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender hashes the whole packet with fields that routers change blanked out, and the receiver hashes it again and compares. If they do not match, the packet is thrown away and the failure is logged.

sections.title: Conformance Requirements
sections.content: Implementations that claim conformance or compliance with this specification MUST fully implement the header described here, MUST support manual key distribution for use with this option, MUST comply with all requirements of the Security Architecture for the Internet Protocol, and MUST support the use of keyed MD5 as described in the companion document IP Authentication using Keyed MD5. Implementations MAY also implement other authentication algorithms. Implementors are advised to consult the most recent version of the IAB Official Standards RFC for further guidance on the status of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: An implementation that claims to follow this document has to support the header, manual key distribution, the security architecture it depends on, and keyed MD5. Other algorithms are optional.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC is explicit that this mechanism is not a panacea for the security issues in any internetwork, but it does provide a component useful in building a secure internetwork. The quality of the security provided depends completely on the strength of the cryptographic algorithm implemented, the strength of the key, the correctness of the algorithm's implementation, the security of the key management mechanism and its implementation, and the correctness of the Authentication Header and IP implementations in all participating systems. If any of these assumptions fail, little or no real security is provided. Implementors are encouraged to use high assurance methods to develop the security relevant parts of their products.

Users interested in confidentiality should consider the IP Encapsulating Security Payload instead of or in conjunction with this specification, and users seeking protection from traffic analysis might consider appropriate link encryption. One particular issue is that a packet which causes an error to be reported back via ICMP might be so large as not to fit entirely within the ICMP message returned, in which case the receiver of the ICMP message might not be able to independently authenticate the returned portion. That means the host might either trust an unauthenticated ICMP message, which might create a security problem, or not trust and hence not react appropriately to a legitimate ICMP message. Similar complications arise if an encrypted packet causes an ICMP error message to be sent and that packet is truncated.

Active attacks are widely known to exist in the Internet, so unauthenticated source routing is a significant security risk unless all received source routed packets are authenticated using the Authentication Header or some other cryptographic mechanism. The use of IP tunneling with AH also creates multiple pairs of endpoints that might perform AH processing, and implementers and administrators should carefully consider the impacts of tunneling on the authenticity of received tunneled packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The header only protects a packet if the algorithm, the key and the key management are all sound. It also cannot authenticate an ICMP error message that has been truncated to fit in a smaller packet, so some error reports can only be half trusted.

fields.name: Next Header
fields.desc: Identifies the next payload after the Authentication Header.

fields.name: Payload Length
fields.desc: Length of the Authentication Data field in 32-bit words; the minimum is 0.

fields.name: RESERVED
fields.desc: Reserved for future use; must be set to all zeros when sent.

fields.name: Security Parameters Index
fields.desc: Identifies the security association for this datagram; 0 means no security association exists.

fields.name: Authentication Data
fields.desc: A variable number of 32-bit words holding the algorithm output.

viz.caption: FIELDS TREATED AS ZERO FOR THE AUTHENTICATION CALCULATION

items.title: IPv4 Time to Live
items.text: Set to all zeros for the calculation; all other IPv4 base header fields are processed normally.

items.title: IPv4 Header Checksum
items.text: Set to all zeros for the calculation.

items.title: IPv6 Hop Limit
items.text: The only IPv6 base header field handled specially.

items.title: Authentication Data field
items.text: Considered to be filled with zeros while the digest is computed.

items.title: IPv6 option type bit
items.text: The third-highest-order bit decides whether the option is included or replaced by zero bits.

cells: After the Hop-by-Hop and Routing headers, before the Destination Options.
